title: Never Changes Direction
statement:
You get an integer array nums. Return true if it only ever goes one way: either every value is at least the one before it, or every value is at most the one before it. Equal neighbours are allowed in both cases.

Otherwise return false.

examples.why: It never goes down. The flat step 2 → 2 is fine.
It never goes up. The first step is flat, so it tells you nothing about the direction yet.
It goes up from 2 to 3 and then down to 1.

hints: You do not know the direction in advance, and a flat start does not reveal it.
Instead of guessing, record two facts as you walk: did you ever see a step up, and did you ever see a step down?
The array is fine as long as it has not seen both.

explain.intuition:
The only way to fail is to see at least one step up and at least one step down somewhere in the array. Flat steps never matter. So walk once, set a flag when a step goes up and another when a step goes down, and answer !(up && down).

This avoids the tempting bug of fixing the direction from the first two values, which breaks when they are equal.
steps: For each i from 1: if nums[i] > nums[i − 1] set up; if nums[i] < nums[i − 1] set down.
If both are set you can stop early and return false.
pitfalls: Deciding the direction from nums[0] and nums[1]. In [2, 2, 3, 1] they are equal, and the real direction appears later.
Using strict comparisons for the whole check (< instead of ≤), which rejects flat steps like in [5, 5, 5].

solutions.title: Check both directions separately
solutions.idea: Test whether the array is non-decreasing, then whether it is non-increasing.

solutions.title: One pass with two flags
solutions.idea: Remember whether a step up and a step down have been seen. Both means false.

followups: Return the length of the longest stretch that never changes direction.
The values arrive as a stream. What is the least state you need to answer after each new value?
